title: So You Want to Put a Center on Stephon Castle
contentHtml:
One goal of this space is to elaborate on topics that come up on The Zach Lowe Show but don’t get much room to breathe—especially X’s-and-O’s detail that lends itself better to writing.

To wit: I mentioned on Monday’s episode that Saturday’s San Antonio Spurs–Portland Trail Blazers game was a one-night tutorial in all the ways the Spurs, now 9-2 with the league’s best point differential, can attack the most interesting and perhaps consequential strategic battleground in the league: when opponents stash their centers on Stephon Castle and use wings to defend Victor Wembanyama.

Portland has a lot of experience with this gambit, having tried it for much of their first-round series with San Antonio last postseason. Hiding slower centers on Castle keeps them out of San Antonio’s primary pick-and-roll actions, which obviously feature Wembanyama, the league’s most dangerous screen-and-dive fiend. Long, physical wings can get into Wembanyama’s body, annoying him the way Stephen Jackson once irritated Dirk Nowitzki. They can also switch more pick-and-rolls when the Spurs use Wembanyama as their screener, since wings assigned to Wembanyama should be able to track San Antonio’s ball handlers.

The strategy invites Castle to shoot, and it’s probably not ideal that 44 percent of his attempts this season have been 3s—up from 30 percent last season and 34 percent in his rookie year. (In fairness, this season’s share was over 50 percent a week or so ago, so it’s already ticking down.)

Castle can neuter this strategy by improving as a shooter. Castle attempts 6.2 3s per game; of those, 5.5 are classified as “wide open,” per the NBA—the most among all players. He has hit 36.7 percent of those attempts—solid, but not good enough to yank opponents out of their centers-on-Castle defense. Among almost 250 players who have jacked at least 20 3s this season, only four have had more distance on average between themselves and their nearest defender upon shooting than Castle, per GeniusIQ tracking data: Ron Holland II, Wendell Carter Jr., Jake LaRavia, and John Collins. (Two Pistons!)

The Spurs can (and sometimes do) stash Castle in the corner, meaning he’ll at least have a shorter and easier 3 if centers abandon him.

Depending on the alignment of the floor, I’d like to see Castle eat up all the space centers concede to him—for Castle to pull the ball out, rev up, and zoom right into those guys. That’s another counter.

The floor is a little more crowded now than last year, with the Spurs starting all three of Castle, De’Aaron Fox, and Dylan Harper—swapping the latter in for a spot-up ace in Julian Champagnie. That lineup is undeniably working; the Spurs are a ridiculous plus-69 in 105 minutes with their starting five on the floor. The three point guards play together only when Wembanyama is also on the court, and he can make any lineup soar.

The amount of off-the-bounce juice in those groups is really hard to deal with; they can absolutely fly in transition, since almost anyone can push off misses and turnovers. Most swing passes find someone who has been the no. 1 ballhandling option at some point in his life. If this keeps up, there will be no reason to tweak the starting five even once Tobias Harris returns from a calf injury to round out San Antonio’s wing rotation. If the group hums, the benefit of keeping all the young cornerstones happy outweighs any concerns about spacing. The guard trio is logging only about 11 minutes per game anyway.

That said, there will be matchups and maybe playoff series in which Mitch Johnson will have to think harder about how long they should play together and which lineups should close games. There will come a night, maybe soon, in which he sits one of the three point guards in crunch time of a national TV game in favor of a second outside shooter. (He could also choose to sit Devin Vassell, the only true spot-up option in the starting five, but that is a different kind of adjustment.)

How San Antonio navigates the centers-on-Castle strategy on any particular night might play into those knotty decisions. The Spurs have spent dozens of games over multiple seasons mastering a pile of counters that go beyond “Please shoot well and drive hard, Stephon.”
